description: Multi-turn memory stress benchmark: implicit dependencies, topic shifts, conflicting updates, cross-session isolation. Pair with tests/memory_benchmark_runner.py. Conversations avoid meta phrases about testing memory.

protocol.memory_trigger_note: chatbotAgent triggers mem0 extraction when hybrid session message count is divisible by 12. Place durable facts in early turns so they are inside the first extraction window when possible.
protocol.auth_and_trace: Same as rag_evaluator: EVAL_BASE_URL, EVAL_AUTH_TOKEN or server SKIP_AUTH, ALLOW_EVAL_TRACE=true for memory_context_preview in eval_trace.
protocol.evaluation_strictness: Heuristic token/phrase match against eval_trace.memory_context_preview and assistant text on configured turns; supplement with human or LLM-as-judge for production gates.
protocol.groq_memory_judge: With GROQ_API_KEY and MEMORY_BENCHMARK_USE_JUDGE not 0, memory_benchmark_runner attaches llm_deep_diagnostic per conversation (see docs/MEMORY_QUALITY_EVAL_PROTOCOL.md).

conversations.evaluation_focus: Relocate offer, partner climate sensitivity, dog logistics; late turns ask for winter coping and pet move advice without restating Seattle or dog name.
turns: It's been a heavy month — not a crisis, just a lot landing at once.
I finally got an offer for a role I've chased for two years. I'd need to move before the holidays.
The job's in the Pacific Northwest — basically Seattle metro if I accept.
My girlfriend says she's happy for me but I hear something else when she talks about the gray season.
She grew up in southern Arizona — sun every day — so months of drizzle aren't abstract to her.
We adopted a nervous little dog last year, Miso, who's only known our cramped Austin walk-up.
I've been doom-scrolling rental listings with fenced yards and feeling stupid for how much that calms me.
The new team feels competent. Less reorg theater than where I am now.
My boss took me out for coffee and danced around whether I'm leaving. Exhausting.
I swing between wanting to say yes tomorrow and lying awake wondering if I'm dragging someone into a mistake.
Can you help me separate what's normal big-decision noise from a signal I'm ignoring something important?
I don't need cheerleading — I want a frame for the tradeoffs that doesn't turn into me catastrophizing.
When I picture February I see her miserable in a rain shell waiting for me while I'm stuck on a late call.
If we go — what are a few concrete first-winter things that aren't just buy a lamp and hope?
Anything you'd actually do before moving a skittish dog halfway across the country?
I'm drafting a short note to myself about what I'm scared of losing if we go — can you suggest one honest sentence that doesn't use anyone's name?
conversations.implicit_dependency_notes: Turns 13–16 should lean on prior context (climate, partner mood, dog) without user repeating full backstory.

conversations.evaluation_focus: Early technical goal and deadline; mid-topic shift to cooking; later implicit tie-back to injury and milestone without naming stack explicitly in the question.

The soup was a coconut lentil thing — too thin at first, fixed it with peanut butter.
Kitchen victory made me realize I've been sitting like a gargoyle at the desk though.
My right wrist has been complaining for weeks — brace during the day, ice at night.
Typing through it feels stupid but I don't want to push the deadline again.
Work email is a separate dumpster fire — politics about a roadmap slide I didn't even own.
I took a long walk at lunch listening to a podcast about nothing related to code. Helped a little.
If I ignore the wrist entirely I'll pay for it — already dropped a coffee mug once.
Can you give me a brutally honest read on whether the Friday demo is realistic if I protect the wrist?

conversations.evaluation_focus: User states long-term vegetarianism then later adds fish; final social scenario should follow updated diet not stale rule.
turns: I've been vegetarian for about five years — mostly ethics, partly digestion.
Family holidays are fine; work lunches are where I get weird energy from people.
Someone always jokes I'm going to 'wither' without protein. Old joke, still annoying.
I started lifting heavier this year and got sloppy about meal planning.
Met with a dietitian who wasn't preachy — suggested tracking iron and B12 seriously.
For the last month I've actually been eating fish a couple times a week — mostly salmon, nothing dramatic.
I haven't updated my Slack bio or whatever — feels silly but also I'm dreading the commentary.
My running group does a big Saturday breakfast after long miles — bacon everywhere, you know the vibe.
I don't want to be the person with a speech at the table.
Also my partner eats everything — no conflict there, just me in my own head.
Work is slow this week so I'm over-rotating on this instead of doing something useful.
Can you help me script a one-liner if someone pushes the old vegetarian joke after they've seen me order fish?
I want it firm but not lecture-y — these are friends, not internet strangers.
If someone offers bacon at brunch and I say no, what's a casual line that doesn't invite a debate?
Separate question: any low-drama way to correct someone who still tells new people I'm strict veg?
Tiny check — based on what I said about fish, does 'strict vegetarian' even apply to me anymore, language-wise?
conversations.implicit_dependency_notes: Turn 16 checks updated self-description; assistant should not insist on strict vegetarian if user clarified fish.
